title: Decomposing the 'trust science too much' backfire
why: Addresses the design and power causes: it replaces bundled stimuli with a manipulated mechanism and concentrates sample on the one robust effect.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of -0.17 for the video; the pooled SD implied by the SEs is about 0.9. The ~0.12 MDE allows for shrinkage of the original estimate, and the power table gives no contrasts.

rationale: In the source study the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.17 points (SE 0.046, p<0.001), but it bundles fallibility framing, video format and a particular source (vlogbrothers). Other arms were small (about 120 respondents in some), so the cause of the drop cannot be isolated. This design manipulates each feature directly and adds a one-week re-measure.
contribution: Identifies whether fallibility content, video format or source drives the one robust negative effect on trust in science, and whether it persists.
hypothesis: The original video lowers trust relative to control, and the drop is mainly due to the fallibility segment: the no-fallibility video and the neutral video will not lower trust, and the transcript will lower trust by a similar amount to the video.
primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science: mean of the 6-item scale (items 4-6 reverse-coded), 5-point.
comparison: Each arm versus pure control, adjusting for pre-treatment trust; original video versus no-fallibility video (fallibility effect); original video versus transcript (format effect); no-fallibility video versus neutral video (source/other content); one-week outcome analysed the same way.
unresolved: Actual video files, edited no-fallibility cut, transcript and neutral video must be supplied by the research team.
Delayed one-week follow-up wave must be fielded separately; its instrument repeats the post-trust items.
label: Design advance

title: Do the small positive videos replicate across samples and baseline trust?
why: Addresses the multiplicity and sample causes: a confirmatory replication of the three positive arms with a single correction, plus a test of where the effect holds.

power_target.basis: Observed +0.06 effects for videos 12, 15 and 20, with SD about 0.9; 80% power at alpha 0.05 needs roughly 3,500-4,400 per arm. A single contrast is not computed in the power table.

rationale: Videos 12, 15 and 20 raised trust by about 0.06 (Video 12 CI [0.005, 0.123]; Video 15 CI [0.014, 0.112]) among 32 uncorrected tests, with intervals near zero. A confirmatory replication in a new panel with few tests, plus moderation by baseline trust and party, tests whether the effects are real and where they hold.
contribution: Provides a pre-registered, multiplicity-limited replication of three small positive video effects in a non-Lucid sample and tests moderation by baseline trust and party.
hypothesis: Videos 12, 15 and 20 each raise post-treatment trust in science relative to control by about 0.06 points; effects differ by baseline trust (low vs high) and party identification.
primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science, mean of the 6 items with items 4-6 reverse-coded, adjusted for pre-treatment trust.
comparison: Each of Videos 12, 15 and 20 vs control (three one-sided tests, Holm-corrected); exploratory arm x baseline trust (median split) and arm x party interactions; the comparison video is a benchmark for the negative effect.
unresolved: The actual video files for videos 12, 15, 20 and the comparison video must be supplied by the research team.
